Linear Algebra and Geometry · Channels A, B and C · Lesson L01

Real numbers

Where the numbers we will use throughout the course come from: the sets N⊊Z⊊Q⊊R\N \subsetneq \Z \subsetneq \Q \subsetneq \RN⊊Z⊊Q⊊R, how the real numbers are built, why 2\sqrt 22​ is not a fraction, the nine rules that make R\RR a field, order and the brackets not to confuse. Plus: the symbols of mathematical language and calculations with roots without a calculator, which you need in every exam.

Handouts
lesson 1 · pp. 2–5
Book
Martelli, §1.1 and complement 1.II
Lecturers
Reto Buzano and Marco Radeschi · A.Y. 2026/27
Study time
90–120 minutes
  • Definition or result to know
  • Pitfall / typical mistake
  • Matters in the exam
  • Beyond the handouts
  • Worked example
  • The idea and the method, step by step

The lesson in 8 points

  • The numbers of the course live in sets nested one inside the other: N={0,1,2,… }\N = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}N={0,1,2,…} (zero is included!), then Z\ZZ with the negatives, Q\QQ with the fractions, R\RR with all the real numbers; from the next lesson also C\CC. We write N⊊Z⊊Q⊊R\N \subsetneq \Z \subsetneq \Q \subsetneq \RN⊊Z⊊Q⊊R.
  • Each new set is needed to solve equations that had no solution before: x+5=3x + 5 = 3x+5=3 cannot be solved in N\NN, 2x=12x = 12x=1 cannot be solved in Z\ZZ, x2=2x^2 = 2x2=2 cannot be solved in Q\QQ.
  • A real number is a number with infinitely many digits after the decimal point. To define it precisely we use Cauchy sequences: infinite lists of fractions that, as you go on, get as close to one another as you like.
  • R\RR is complete: it has no "holes". Q\QQ instead has lots of them, for example where 2\sqrt 22​, π\piπ and eee are.
  • 2\sqrt 22​ is not a fraction: it is the first proof by contradiction of the course, one you should be able to redo.
  • Sum and product in R\RR obey nine rules (identity elements, opposites, inverses, commutative, associative and distributive properties). A set with these rules is called a field: Q\QQ, R\RR and C\CC are fields, N\NN and Z\ZZ are not.
  • R\RR is ordered: a>ba > ba>b means that a−ba - ba−b is positive.
  • Different brackets, different objects: {1,2}\{1, 2\}{1,2} is a set of two numbers, (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2) is an open interval (or a point of the plane), [1,2][1, 2][1,2] is a closed interval.

Linear Algebra and Geometry uses the same handouts in the three channels: Buzano teaches in channels A and B, Radeschi in channels B and C. These notes follow the 2026 handouts, so they hold in the same way for A, B and C. Only the days of the lessons change: the course's Moodle page (MDAG2, id 3831) warns that timetable changes are announced there and in class. Exam and quiz are the same for the three channels.

§1

Sets: the starting language

p. 2

Before numbers we need a word: set. A set is a collection of objects, called its elements. For example the students in a classroom form a set, and each student is an element of that set.

In mathematics a set is written with curly brackets { }\{\ \}{ } (braces), putting the elements inside, separated by commas:

A={1,3,5}A = \{1, 3, 5\}A={1,3,5}

This AAA contains exactly three numbers: 1, 3 and 5. When the elements are infinitely many, you write a few of them and then the dots …\dots…, which mean "and so on, with the same rule".

Beyond the handouts · two rules about braces

In a set order does not matter and repetitions do not matter: {1,2}\{1, 2\}{1,2}, {2,1}\{2, 1\}{2,1} and {1,1,2}\{1, 1, 2\}{1,1,2} are the same set, with two elements. Only what is inside counts. This is why braces must never be used for points or vectors, where order matters a lot (see the section on notation).

The symbols you will use right away

SymbolRead asExampleTrue or false?
x∈Ax \in Ax∈A"xxx belongs to AAA"3∈{1,3,5}3 \in \{1, 3, 5\}3∈{1,3,5}true
x∉Ax \notin Ax∈/A"xxx does not belong to AAA"2∉{1,3,5}2 \notin \{1, 3, 5\}2∈/{1,3,5}true
B⊂AB \subset AB⊂A"BBB is contained in AAA" (every element of BBB is also in AAA){1,5}⊂{1,3,5}\{1, 5\} \subset \{1, 3, 5\}{1,5}⊂{1,3,5}true
B⊊AB \subsetneq AB⊊A"BBB is strictly contained in AAA" (B⊂AB \subset AB⊂A and AAA has at least one element more){1,5}⊊{1,3,5}\{1, 5\} \subsetneq \{1, 3, 5\}{1,5}⊊{1,3,5}true: 3 is the extra one
∅\emptyset∅"empty set" (no elements)∅⊂A\emptyset \subset A∅⊂A for every set AAAtrue

A set can also be described by a property, instead of listing its elements:

{x∈R∣1<x<2}\{x \in \R \mid 1 < x < 2\}{x∈R∣1<x<2}

reads: "the set of the xxx in R\RR such that 1<x<21 < x < 21<x<2". The bar ∣\mid∣ means precisely "such that" (some people use a colon ::: instead). To the left of the bar is where the elements are looked for, to the right the condition they must satisfy.

Note · Where to go deeper

The handouts point out that set theory is covered in detail in the Discrete Mathematics part of the course (MDAG part 1). Here only sets of numbers are needed.

§2

Natural numbers, integers and rational numbers

p. 2

Definition 1.1 · Natural numbers, integers and rational numbers

The set of natural numbers is N={0,1,2,3,… }\N = \{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\}N={0,1,2,3,…}.

If we add the negative numbers we obtain the set of integers Z={…,−2,−1,0,1,2,… }\Z = \{\dots, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, \dots\}Z={…,−2,−1,0,1,2,…}.

If besides the integers we consider all numbers that can be written as fractions ab\frac abba​, we obtain the set of rational numbers

Q={ab ; a,b∈Z, b≠0}.\Q = \left\{ \frac ab \ ;\ a, b \in \Z,\ b \neq 0 \right\}.Q={ba​ ; a,b∈Z, b=0}.

Let us look at the definition one piece at a time.

  • N\NN are the numbers for counting: 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on, without end.
  • Z\ZZ adds the negatives: −1,−2,−3,…-1, -2, -3, \dots−1,−2,−3,… The symbol comes from the German Zahlen, "numbers".
  • Q\QQ contains all fractions ab\frac abba​ with aaa and bbb integers. The condition b≠0b \neq 0b=0 is there because you cannot divide by zero. The Q stands for quotient.
  • In Q\QQ the semicolon inside the braces does the same job as the bar: "where aaa and bbb are integers and bbb is not zero".

Pitfall · Zero is a natural number

In this course (and in Martelli's book) N\NN starts from 0. In some school books N\NN starts from 1: at the exam the course's convention applies.

Why we need ever larger sets

One thread links all these sets: each time we find a simple equation that has no solution in the set we have, and so we enlarge it.

EquationSolutionIn the old set?New set
x+5=3x + 5 = 3x+5=3x=−2x = -2x=−2−2∉N-2 \notin \N−2∈/NZ\ZZ
2x=12x = 12x=1x=12x = \frac 12x=21​12∉Z\frac 12 \notin \Z21​∈/ZQ\QQ
x2=2x^2 = 2x2=2x=±2x = \pm\sqrt 2x=±2​2∉Q\sqrt 2 \notin \Q2​∈/Q (we prove it later)R\RR
x2=−1x^2 = -1x2=−1no real numberno real square is negativeC\CC, from lesson L02

One fraction, many ways to write it

The same rational number can be written in infinitely many ways:

17=321=−8−56\frac 17 = \frac 3{21} = \frac{-8}{-56}71​=213​=−56−8​

All three are worth "one seventh". To build Q\QQ precisely we have to declare that these fractions represent the same number: this is done with an equivalence relation, a concept you will study properly in Discrete Mathematics. In practice the rule is:

ab=cd⟺ad=bc.\frac ab = \frac cd \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad ad = bc.ba​=dc​⟺ad=bc.

Let us check with 17\frac 1771​ and 321\frac 3{21}213​: 1⋅21=211 \cdot 21 = 211⋅21=21 and 7⋅3=217 \cdot 3 = 217⋅3=21. Equal, so they are the same fraction.

Note · What comes first

The handouts specify that N\NN is a primitive concept: it is not defined from anything else, you start from it. Then Z\ZZ is built from N\NN, and Q\QQ from Z\ZZ.

Beyond the handouts · fractions in decimal form

If you do the division, every fraction becomes a decimal number that is either terminating or repeating, that is with a group of digits that repeats forever:

14=0.2513=0.333…=0.3‾17=0.142857‾\frac 14 = 0.25 \qquad \frac 13 = 0.333\ldots = 0.\overline{3} \qquad \frac 17 = 0.\overline{142857}41​=0.2531​=0.333…=0.371​=0.142857

The converse holds too: every repeating decimal is a fraction (exercise 2). So a number with infinitely many digits that never repeat cannot be rational: those are exactly the irrational numbers.

§3

From school to a precise definition of the real numbers

pp. 2–3

The school idea: infinitely many digits after the point

At school you learn that a real number is a number that can have infinitely many digits after the decimal point, like π=3.14159…\pi = 3.14159\ldotsπ=3.14159… The handouts say that this definition is correct, with just one ambiguity to remember: two different writings can denote the same number. For example

5.9739‾=5.9739999…=5.974.5.973\overline{9} = 5.9739999\ldots = 5.974.5.9739=5.9739999…=5.974.

The same happens with 0.9‾=0.999…0.\overline 9 = 0.999\ldots0.9=0.999…, which is exactly 111. A simple way to convince yourself:

  1. we know that 13=0.333…\frac 13 = 0.333\ldots31​=0.333…;
  2. multiply both sides by 3: on the left 3⋅13=13 \cdot \frac 13 = 13⋅31​=1, on the right every digit 3 becomes 9;
  3. so 1=0.999…1 = 0.999\ldots1=0.999…

It is not "a number just below 1": it is exactly 1, written in another way.

The problem: how do you add infinitely many digits?

The school definition, however, does not say how to do the operations. To add two numbers you start from the rightmost digits, with carries. But with infinitely many digits there is no rightmost digit to start from. A different way of defining the reals is needed, which the handouts take from analysis and which has an extra merit: it does not depend on base 10 (which we use, the lecturers write, only because we have ten fingers).

Sequences

A sequence is an infinite list of numbers, one for each position 1,2,3,…1, 2, 3, \dots1,2,3,…:

a1, a2, a3, a4, …a_1,\ a_2,\ a_3,\ a_4,\ \dotsa1​, a2​, a3​, a4​, …

It is denoted by (an)(a_n)(an​). The number ana_nan​ is called the term in position nnn: a1a_1a1​ is the first, a2a_2a2​ the second, and so on.

Cauchy sequences

The idea is simple. Take a sequence of fractions that, as it goes on, tightens up: after a while the terms are all very close to one another, as close as you like. The precise definition says this, with symbols.

Definition · Cauchy sequence (p. 2)

A sequence (an)(a_n)(an​) of rational numbers an∈Qa_n \in \Qan​∈Q is a Cauchy sequence if for every rational number ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 there is an N>0N > 0N>0 such that

∣am−an∣<εfor all m,n>N.|a_m - a_n| < \varepsilon \quad \text{for all } m, n > N.∣am​−an​∣<εfor all m,n>N.

Piece by piece:

  • ε\varepsilonε (the Greek letter epsilon) is a tolerance: a positive number as small as you like, for example 0.010.010.01 or 0.0000010.0000010.000001.
  • ∣am−an∣|a_m - a_n|∣am​−an​∣ is the distance between two terms: the absolute value ∣⋅∣|\cdot|∣⋅∣ removes the sign.
  • "there is an NNN such that … for all m,n>Nm, n > Nm,n>N" means: from some point on (after position NNN), any pair of terms is less than ε\varepsilonε apart.
  • You choose the tolerance, and the definition must work for every choice: the smaller ε\varepsilonε is, the further on you will have to go (the larger NNN will be).

Example 1.2 · The number π\piπ

The number π=3.1415926…\pi = 3.1415926\ldotsπ=3.1415926… corresponds to the sequence of rational numbers

a1=3.1a2=3.14a3=3.141a4=3.1415…a_1 = 3.1 \quad a_2 = 3.14 \quad a_3 = 3.141 \quad a_4 = 3.1415 \quad \dotsa1​=3.1a2​=3.14a3​=3.141a4​=3.1415…

Each ana_nan​ is rational: for example a2=3.14=314100a_2 = 3.14 = \frac{314}{100}a2​=3.14=100314​. And it is a Cauchy sequence: after position nnn all the terms have the same first n+1n + 1n+1 digits, so they are less than 10−n10^{-n}10−n apart. For example from a3a_3a3​ on the terms all start with 3.1413.1413.141, and are less than 0.0010.0010.001 apart.

The sequence that defines a real number is not unique: 3.2; 3.15; 3.142; 3.1416; …3.2;\ 3.15;\ 3.142;\ 3.1416;\ \dots3.2; 3.15; 3.142; 3.1416; … (the approximations from above) also works, because its difference from the previous sequence tends to zero.

The real numbers, at last

Definition · Real numbers (p. 3)

The real numbers are defined as equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences of rational numbers. Two Cauchy sequences are equivalent if their difference is a sequence that tends to zero.

Less abstractly, the procedure works like this. Take a Cauchy sequence of rational numbers:

  • if it converges to a rational number a∞a_\inftya∞​ (that is, it gets closer and closer to that number), it simply represents that number a∞a_\inftya∞​;
  • if it does not converge to any rational number, it "would like" to tend to something that does not exist in Q\QQ: then it defines a new number, which is not in Q\QQ. It is an irrational number.

As a picture: Q\QQ is like a ruler with infinitely many marks, but full of microscopic holes. A Cauchy sequence that "points" to a hole serves to fill it.

Example 1.3 · The number eee

The sequence of rational numbers

an=(1+1n)na_n = \left(1 + \frac 1n\right)^nan​=(1+n1​)n

is a Cauchy sequence but does not converge to a rational number. So it defines a new real number: Euler's number e=2.71828…e = 2.71828\ldotse=2.71828…

Let us compute the first terms, to see that they really are fractions:

a1=(1+1)1=2,a2=(32)2=94=2.25,a3=(43)3=6427≈2.370.a_1 = (1 + 1)^1 = 2, \qquad a_2 = \left(\frac 32\right)^2 = \frac 94 = 2.25, \qquad a_3 = \left(\frac 43\right)^3 = \frac{64}{27} \approx 2.370.a1​=(1+1)1=2,a2​=(23​)2=49​=2.25,a3​=(34​)3=2764​≈2.370.

Completeness: R has no holes (p. 3)

Intuitively you can work with two ideas:

  1. every real number can be approximated by rational numbers, with any precision you want (as 3.141593.141593.14159 approximates π\piπ);
  2. with this construction we have plugged all the holes between the rational numbers.

The second idea has a precise name.

Proposition · R\RR is complete

Unlike Q\QQ, the set R\RR of real numbers is complete: every Cauchy sequence in R\RR converges.

It means that, if we redid the whole construction starting from sequences of real numbers instead of rational ones, we would not add any new number: all the holes have already been filled.

Beyond the handouts · where to find it in the book

Martelli's book presents this construction in complement 1.II "Costruzione dei numeri reali" (pp. 40–42 of the book). In the two 2026 exam sessions (15/01 and 07/09) there are no questions on the construction of R\RR: at the exam you mostly need the sets, the notation and the field properties.

§4

Irrational numbers: why 2\sqrt 22​ is not a fraction

p. 4

Let us sum up the sets seen so far:

N⊊Z⊊Q⊊R\N \subsetneq \Z \subsetneq \Q \subsetneq \RN⊊Z⊊Q⊊R

Each inclusion is strict (⊊\subsetneq⊊): each set has at least one element that the previous one lacks. To prove it one example per step is enough: −1∈Z-1 \in \Z−1∈Z but −1∉N-1 \notin \N−1∈/N; 12∈Q\frac 12 \in \Q21​∈Q but 12∉Z\frac 12 \notin \Z21​∈/Z; 2∈R\sqrt 2 \in \R2​∈R but 2∉Q\sqrt 2 \notin \Q2​∈/Q. The last example is the trickiest, and it has to be proved.

Where does 2\sqrt 22​ come from? From a square with side 1: by Pythagoras' theorem its diagonal measures 12+12=2\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt 212+12​=2​. It is a length you can draw perfectly well, and yet it is not a fraction.

Proof by contradiction

To prove that something is true by contradiction you proceed like this:

  1. you assume that the opposite is true;
  2. you reason correctly, step by step;
  3. you reach a contradiction, that is something impossible;
  4. so the assumption of step 1 was wrong, and the claim is true.

Martelli sums it up like this: you negate the claim and show that this leads to an absurdity; then the claim cannot be false, and so it is true by exclusion.

Proposition 1.4

The number 2\sqrt 22​ is not rational.

Here is the proof from the handouts, with every step explained.

  1. Suppose, for a contradiction, that 2\sqrt 22​ is rational. Then 2=ab\sqrt 2 = \frac ab2​=ba​ with a,ba, ba,b integers and b≠0b \neq 0b=0.
  2. We can assume that the fraction is reduced to lowest terms, that is that aaa and bbb have no common factors: if they had any, we would just simplify it. This point is important: we are about to contradict it.
  3. Square: 2=a2b22 = \frac{a^2}{b^2}2=b2a2​. Multiply both sides by b2b^2b2:
    a2=2b2.a^2 = 2b^2.a2=2b2.
  4. Then a2a^2a2 is even, because it is twice an integer (b2b^2b2).
  5. Then aaa is even too. Why? If aaa were odd, that is a=2k+1a = 2k + 1a=2k+1, we would have a2=4k2+4k+1=2(2k2+2k)+1a^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1a2=4k2+4k+1=2(2k2+2k)+1, which is odd. So aaa cannot be odd.
  6. Being even, a=2ka = 2ka=2k for some integer kkk, and so a2=4k2a^2 = 4k^2a2=4k2. Substituting in step 3: 4k2=2b24k^2 = 2b^24k2=2b2, that is, dividing by 2,
    b2=2k2.b^2 = 2k^2.b2=2k2.
  7. With the same reasoning as steps 4 and 5, b2b^2b2 is even too and so bbb is even.
  8. But then aaa and bbb are both even: they have the factor 2 in common, and the fraction ab\frac abba​ was not reduced to lowest terms. This contradicts step 2.
  9. The assumption "2\sqrt 22​ is rational" leads to a contradiction, so it is false: 2\sqrt 22​ is not rational. □\square□
Proof · another route, from Martelli's book

Martelli too reaches a2=2b2a^2 = 2b^2a2=2b2 and then uses the prime factorisation. In a square every prime factor appears an even number of times (for example 36=22⋅3236 = 2^2 \cdot 3^236=22⋅32). So in a2a^2a2 the factor 2 appears an even number of times, while in 2b22b^22b2 it appears an odd number of times (those of b2b^2b2, which are even, plus one). Two equal numbers have the same factorisation, so a2=2b2a^2 = 2b^2a2=2b2 is impossible: twice a square is never a square.

The idea · the method, to remember

Three ingredients: (1) write the number as a reduced fraction; (2) square and clear the denominators; (3) show that aaa and bbb have a common factor. With the same recipe you prove that 3\sqrt 33​, 5\sqrt 55​, 6\sqrt 66​ are not rational (exercises 4 and 9).

Beyond the handouts · other irrational numbers

π\piπ and eee are irrational too, but the proofs are much harder and are not needed in the course. In general n\sqrt nn​ is irrational whenever nnn is not a perfect square: 4=2\sqrt 4 = 24​=2 and 9=3\sqrt 9 = 39​=3 are integers, while 2\sqrt 22​, 3\sqrt 33​, 5\sqrt 55​, 8\sqrt 88​ are irrational.

Pitfall · Irrational times irrational is not always irrational

2⋅2=2\sqrt 2 \cdot \sqrt 2 = 22​⋅2​=2 and 2+(−2)=0\sqrt 2 + (-\sqrt 2) = 02​+(−2​)=0 are rational. On the other hand a rational plus an irrational is always irrational (exercise 5): for example 1+2∉Q1 + \sqrt 2 \notin \Q1+2​∈/Q.

§5

The properties of R: what a field is

p. 4

On R\RR there are two binary operations: the sum +++ and the product ⋅\cdot⋅. "Binary" means that it takes two numbers and returns one: from 333 and 444 the sum gives 777, the product gives 121212.

Proposition 1.5 · The nine properties of R\RR

On R\RR the operations +++ and ⋅\cdot⋅ have these properties (the symbol ∀\forall∀ reads "for all"):

  1. there is an identity element 000 for addition: 0+a=a+0=a0 + a = a + 0 = a0+a=a+0=a, ∀a∈R\forall a \in \R∀a∈R;
  2. the commutative property holds: a+b=b+aa + b = b + aa+b=b+a, ∀a,b∈R\forall a, b \in \R∀a,b∈R;
  3. the associative property holds: a+(b+c)=(a+b)+ca + (b + c) = (a + b) + ca+(b+c)=(a+b)+c, ∀a,b,c∈R\forall a, b, c \in \R∀a,b,c∈R;
  4. every element a∈Ra \in \Ra∈R has an inverse (or opposite) −a-a−a, such that a+(−a)=(−a)+a=0a + (-a) = (-a) + a = 0a+(−a)=(−a)+a=0;
  5. there is an identity element 111 for multiplication: 1⋅a=a⋅1=a1 \cdot a = a \cdot 1 = a1⋅a=a⋅1=a, ∀a∈R\forall a \in \R∀a∈R;
  6. the commutative property holds: a⋅b=b⋅aa \cdot b = b \cdot aa⋅b=b⋅a, ∀a,b∈R\forall a, b \in \R∀a,b∈R;
  7. the associative property holds: a⋅(b⋅c)=(a⋅b)⋅ca \cdot (b \cdot c) = (a \cdot b) \cdot ca⋅(b⋅c)=(a⋅b)⋅c, ∀a,b,c∈R\forall a, b, c \in \R∀a,b,c∈R;
  8. every element a∈Ra \in \Ra∈R with a≠0a \neq 0a=0 has an inverse a−1a^{-1}a−1, such that a⋅a−1=a−1⋅a=1a \cdot a^{-1} = a^{-1} \cdot a = 1a⋅a−1=a−1⋅a=1;
  9. the distributive property holds: a⋅(b+c)=a⋅b+a⋅ca \cdot (b + c) = a \cdot b + a \cdot ca⋅(b+c)=a⋅b+a⋅c, ∀a,b,c∈R\forall a, b, c \in \R∀a,b,c∈R.

The first four are about the sum, 5 to 8 about the product, 9 links them. Here is what they say, with numbers:

#In wordsWith numbers
1adding 0 changes nothing0+7=70 + 7 = 70+7=7
2the order of the addends does not matter2+5=5+2=72 + 5 = 5 + 2 = 72+5=5+2=7
3how you group the addends does not matter1+(2+3)=(1+2)+3=61 + (2 + 3) = (1 + 2) + 3 = 61+(2+3)=(1+2)+3=6
4every number has an opposite, which added gives 07+(−7)=07 + (-7) = 07+(−7)=0
5multiplying by 1 changes nothing1⋅7=71 \cdot 7 = 71⋅7=7
6the order of the factors does not matter2⋅5=5⋅2=102 \cdot 5 = 5 \cdot 2 = 102⋅5=5⋅2=10
7how you group the factors does not matter2⋅(3⋅4)=(2⋅3)⋅4=242 \cdot (3 \cdot 4) = (2 \cdot 3) \cdot 4 = 242⋅(3⋅4)=(2⋅3)⋅4=24
8every number other than 0 has an inverse, which multiplied gives 14⋅14=14 \cdot \frac 14 = 14⋅41​=1
9"multiplying a sum" = adding up the products3⋅(2+5)=3⋅2+3⋅5=213 \cdot (2 + 5) = 3 \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot 5 = 213⋅(2+5)=3⋅2+3⋅5=21

Note property 8 carefully: zero has no inverse. There is no number that multiplied by 0 gives 1, because 0⋅x=00 \cdot x = 00⋅x=0 for every xxx. It is again the ban on dividing by zero.

Definition · Field

A set with two operations +++ and ⋅\cdot⋅ that have these nine properties is called a field.

The handouts announce that the concept will come back "in more detail in the future": in lesson L05 the definition of a field is given in general, and from then on the whole course works with vectors "over a field K\KK" (usually K=R\K = \RK=R or K=C\K = \CK=C). Instead of a⋅ba \cdot ba⋅b one often writes just ababab.

Which sets are fields?

Setopposite of every number (4)?inverse of every number ≠0\neq 0=0 (8)?Is it a field?
N\NNno: −3∉N-3 \notin \N−3∈/Nno: 13∉N\frac 13 \notin \N31​∈/Nno
Z\ZZyesno: 12∉Z\frac 12 \notin \Z21​∈/Zno
Q\QQyesyes: the inverse of ab\frac abba​ is ba\frac baab​yes
R\RRyesyesyes
C\CCyesyes (lesson L02)yes

To say that a set is not a field one failing property is enough, with one concrete example: "Z\ZZ is not a field because 222 has no inverse in Z\ZZ" is a complete answer.

Beyond the handouts · a small consequence of the nine rules

From the rules you can also prove what looks obvious, for example that a⋅0=0a \cdot 0 = 0a⋅0=0 for every aaa:

a⋅0=a⋅(0+0)=a⋅0+a⋅0.a \cdot 0 = a \cdot (0 + 0) = a \cdot 0 + a \cdot 0.a⋅0=a⋅(0+0)=a⋅0+a⋅0.

The first step uses rule 1 (0+0=00 + 0 = 00+0=0), the second rule 9. Now add the opposite of a⋅0a \cdot 0a⋅0 to both sides: on the left 000 remains, on the right a⋅0a \cdot 0a⋅0 remains. So a⋅0=0a \cdot 0 = 0a⋅0=0. In lesson L05 the same idea proves that 0v=00v = 00v=0 for a vector vvv (Proposition 5.5).

§6

Order: greater than and less than

p. 5

R\RR, like N\NN, Z\ZZ and Q\QQ, is an ordered set: there is a notion of greater and smaller, and if aaa and bbb are distinct one of the two always holds, a>ba > ba>b or b>ab > ab>a.

The definition uses a trick: instead of comparing any two numbers, it is enough to know which numbers are positive.

Definition · Order (p. 5)

We say that a>ba > ba>b if a−b>0a - b > 0a−b>0.

So to define the order it is enough to make clear which numbers are positive (greater than zero) and which are negative (less than zero).

  • In Z\ZZ the positive numbers are 1,2,3,…1, 2, 3, \dots1,2,3,… For example 7>47 > 47>4 because 7−4=37 - 4 = 37−4=3 is positive.
  • In Q\QQ the positive numbers are the fractions ab\frac abba​ in which aaa and bbb have the same sign: 34\frac 3443​ and −3−4\frac{-3}{-4}−4−3​ are positive, −34\frac{-3}{4}4−3​ is not.
  • In R\RR a number is positive if it is represented by a Cauchy sequence (an)(a_n)(an​) of rationals for which there is a rational ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 with an>εa_n > \varepsilonan​>ε eventually, that is from some position on. In words: the terms, from some point on, all stay above a fixed positive threshold.

Example · why "above a threshold" is needed

The sequence an=1na_n = \frac 1nan​=n1​ has all its terms positive (1, 12, 13, …1,\ \frac 12,\ \frac 13,\ \dots1, 21​, 31​, …), but it tends to zero: it represents the number 000, which is not positive. There is no threshold ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 that the terms exceed forever. On the other hand 3.1; 3.14; 3.141; …3.1;\ 3.14;\ 3.141;\ \dots3.1; 3.14; 3.141; … always stays above the threshold ε=3\varepsilon = 3ε=3, and indeed π>0\pi > 0π>0.

Note · Preview of lesson L02

The complex numbers C\CC form a field, but they are not ordered: between two complex numbers it makes no sense to say which one is greater.

§7

Notation not to confuse

p. 5

Three writings that look similar mean very different things.

WritingWhat it isHow many elementsFor example it contains
{1,2}\{1, 2\}{1,2}the set with exactly the two elements 1 and 22only 1 and 2
(1,2)(1, 2)(1,2)the open interval: all the numbers strictly between 1 and 2, endpoints excludedinfinitely many1.51.51.5 and 1.0011.0011.001, but neither 1 nor 2
[1,2][1, 2][1,2]the closed interval: all the numbers between 1 and 2, endpoints includedinfinitely many111, 1.51.51.5 and 222

With the notation of the first section:

(1,2)={x∈R∣1<x<2},[1,2]={x∈R∣1≤x≤2}.(1, 2) = \{x \in \R \mid 1 < x < 2\}, \qquad [1, 2] = \{x \in \R \mid 1 \le x \le 2\}.(1,2)={x∈R∣1<x<2},[1,2]={x∈R∣1≤x≤2}.

(1,2)(1, 2)(1,2) and [1,2][1, 2][1,2] are sets too, but they contain infinitely many elements.

Beyond the handouts · the other intervals

Brackets can be mixed: [1,2)={x∈R∣1≤x<2}[1, 2) = \{x \in \R \mid 1 \le x < 2\}[1,2)={x∈R∣1≤x<2} includes 1 and excludes 2. For half-lines you use ∞\infty∞, always with a round bracket because ∞\infty∞ is not a number: [0,+∞)={x∈R∣x≥0}[0, +\infty) = \{x \in \R \mid x \ge 0\}[0,+∞)={x∈R∣x≥0}.

There is one last complication: in the course (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2) also denotes a point of the plane R2\R^2R2, or a vector. The same writing can have very different meanings, and the right one is clear from the context:

  • "x∈(1,2)x \in (1, 2)x∈(1,2)" with xxx a real number: it is the interval;
  • "the point P=(1,2)P = (1, 2)P=(1,2)" or "the vector v=(1,2)v = (1, 2)v=(1,2)": it is the ordered pair, with first coordinate 1 and second coordinate 2, and here (1,2)≠(2,1)(1, 2) \neq (2, 1)(1,2)=(2,1).

Matters in the exam · The right notation

The handouts insist: it is essential always to use the right notation. In particular braces are never used for points or vectors: writing {1,2}\{1, 2\}{1,2} for the vector (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2) is a mistake, because in a set order does not matter. In the exam papers column vectors also appear as t(1,2)t(1, 2)t(1,2) or t(1,2){}^t(1, 2)t(1,2), that is "the transpose" of the row (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2): you will see it in lesson L08.

beyond the handouts

Beyond the handouts · why this section

The handouts already use symbols such as ∀\forall∀ and ⟺\Longleftrightarrow⟺ in this lesson. Martelli's book explains them in §1.1 (pp. 4–7). Here is a small dictionary to read formulas out loud.

The quantifiers ∀\forall∀ and ∃\exists∃ change the whole meaning of a sentence, and order matters. Two examples from the book:

  • ∀x∈R ∃y∈R: 2y=x\forall x \in \R\ \exists y \in \R:\ 2y = x∀x∈R ∃y∈R: 2y=x is true: every real number can be divided by 2 (just take y=x2y = \frac x2y=2x​);

Pitfall · "Implies" does not mean "if and only if"

a=2⟹a2=4a = 2 \Longrightarrow a^2 = 4a=2⟹a2=4 is true, but the other way round it is not: a2=4a^2 = 4a2=4 does not imply a=2a = 2a=2, because a=−2a = -2a=−2 works too. When a property holds both ways you write ⟺\Longleftrightarrow⟺.

§10

Calculations with roots without a calculator

beyond the handouts

Matters in the exam · Why now

At the Linear Algebra exam calculators are forbidden, and the quiz answers are often written with roots. In the 07/09/2026 exam the five possible answers for a distance were 333, 33\frac{\sqrt 3}333​​, 333\sqrt 333​, 3\sqrt 33​ and 3+33 + \sqrt 33+3​; for an angle there were arccos⁡343\arccos\frac 3{\sqrt{43}}arccos43​3​, arccos⁡642\arccos\frac 6{\sqrt{42}}arccos42​6​ and similar. You need to recognise at a glance that, for example, 13=33\frac 1{\sqrt 3} = \frac{\sqrt 3}33​1​=33​​.

§11

Towards the exam

exam

The Linear Algebra and Geometry exam (part 2 of MDAG) is written and is the same for channels A, B and C. As of 30/09/2026 the 2026/27 rules have not been published yet (on Moodle: "informazioni seguono", "information to follow"), so the reference is the 2025/26 rules, confirmed by the exam papers:

  • 10 multiple-choice questions, each with 5 answers (a)–(e) and only one correct, 1 point each;
  • 2 open problems with sub-questions, 11 points each: to get partial credit you must show your work;
  • cut-off (sbarramento): the problems are marked only for those who score at least 6 out of 10 in the quiz;
  • 2 hours, maximum 32 points, pass mark 18;
  • materials allowed: only one folded sheet or two A4 sheets (4 sides) handwritten, with formulas, notes and exercises; no calculator and no books;
  • in the quiz the answers are marked with an X, not with a circle.
2026/27 exam sessionRegistration on MyUniToTime and rooms
Fri 22/01/202702/01 – 15/01/202714:00, rooms A, B, C, D, F
Fri 05/02/202716/01 – 29/01/202714:00, rooms A, B, C, D, F

The final MDAG grade is the average of the two tests (Discrete Mathematics and Linear Algebra), which can also be taken in different exam sessions. Careful: sitting again a test you have already passed cancels the previous grade, even if it goes worse. Details and sources in the course sheet.

What of this lesson you need at the exam

  1. Fields. The scalars of vector spaces (lessons L05–L07) live in a field. Being able to say why Z\ZZ is not a field is a typical theory quiz question.
  2. Notation. Sets, intervals, points and vectors with the right brackets: in the problems the answers are written with this notation.
  3. Calculations by hand. Fractions and roots appear in almost every question (norms, angles, distances). Practise now with exercises 2 and 8.
  4. Proofs by contradiction. The quiz does not ask for proofs, but reasoning by contradiction comes back often in the course.

Matters in the exam · The 4-page sheet

It is the only material allowed: it is worth building it lesson by lesson. From this lesson two lines are enough: the rules for roots from the previous section and "field = 9 properties; N\NN and Z\ZZ are not fields".

§12

Quiz

like the exam
  1. Which of these sets, with the usual sum and product, is not a field?
    In Z\ZZ the number 222 has no multiplicative inverse: 12∉Z\frac 12 \notin \Z21​∈/Z. Property 8 fails, so Z\ZZ is not a field. Q\QQ, R\RR and C\CC are.
  2. Which of these numbers is irrational?
    12=23\sqrt{12} = 2\sqrt 312​=23​ and 3\sqrt 33​ is irrational. The others are rational: 0.125=180.125 = \frac 180.125=81​, 9=3\sqrt 9 = 39​=3 and 0.3‾=130.\overline 3 = \frac 130.3=31​; 227\frac{22}7722​ is a fraction (only an approximation of π\piπ).
  3. Which statement is true?
    Each set is strictly contained in the next: −1∈Z∖N-1 \in \Z \setminus \N−1∈Z∖N, 12∈Q∖Z\frac 12 \in \Q \setminus \Z21​∈Q∖Z, 2∈R∖Q\sqrt 2 \in \R \setminus \Q2​∈R∖Q.
  4. The set {x∈R∣1≤x<2}\{x \in \R \mid 1 \le x < 2\}{x∈R∣1≤x<2} is:
    The ≤\le≤ includes 1 (square bracket), the <<< excludes 2 (round bracket). {1,2}\{1, 2\}{1,2} instead is the set with only the two numbers 1 and 2.
  5. The number 0.999…0.999\ldots0.999… (with infinitely many 9s) equals:
    13=0.333…\frac 13 = 0.333\ldots31​=0.333…; multiplying by 3 gives 1=0.999…1 = 0.999\ldots1=0.999…. As with 5.9739‾=5.9745.973\overline 9 = 5.9745.9739=5.974 in the handouts: they are two writings of the same number.
  6. In the proof that 2∉Q\sqrt 2 \notin \Q2​∈/Q, which contradiction is reached?
    From a2=2b2a^2 = 2b^2a2=2b2 it follows that aaa is even, and then that bbb is even too: so aaa and bbb have the factor 2 in common, against the assumption that the fraction was reduced.
  7. Which property does Z\ZZ lack to be a field?
    In Z\ZZ every number has an opposite, and sum and product are commutative, associative and distributive. But only 111 and −1-1−1 have an integer inverse: for example 333 has none.
  8. What is 8+18\sqrt 8 + \sqrt{18}8​+18​?
    8=4⋅2=22\sqrt 8 = \sqrt{4 \cdot 2} = 2\sqrt 28​=4⋅2​=22​ and 18=9⋅2=32\sqrt{18} = \sqrt{9 \cdot 2} = 3\sqrt 218​=9⋅2​=32​, so the sum is 525\sqrt 252​. Careful: 8+18≠26\sqrt 8 + \sqrt{18} \neq \sqrt{26}8​+18​=26​, the root of a sum is not the sum of the roots.
  9. What is a2a_2a2​ in the sequence an=(1+1n)na_n = \left(1 + \frac 1n\right)^nan​=(1+n1​)n? Write a fraction or a decimal.
    9/4
    a2=(1+12)2=(32)2=94=2.25a_2 = \left(1 + \frac 12\right)^2 = \left(\frac 32\right)^2 = \frac 94 = 2.25a2​=(1+21​)2=(23​)2=49​=2.25.

2 · From repeating decimal to fraction basic

Write as a fraction: (a) 0.7‾0.\overline 70.7; (b) 2.3‾2.\overline 32.3; (c) 0.12‾0.\overline{12}0.12.

Solution

The trick: I call the number xxx, multiply it by 101010 (or by 100100100 if the repeating block has two digits) and subtract. The identical infinite tails cancel out.

(a) x=0.777…x = 0.777\ldotsx=0.777…

  • 10x=7.777…10x = 7.777\ldots10x=7.777…
  • 10x−x=7.777…−0.777…=710x - x = 7.777\ldots - 0.777\ldots = 710x−x=7.777…−0.777…=7, that is 9x=79x = 79x=7
  • x=79x = \frac 79x=97​.

(b) x=2.333…x = 2.333\ldotsx=2.333…

  • 10x=23.333…10x = 23.333\ldots10x=23.333…
  • 9x=23.333…−2.333…=219x = 23.333\ldots - 2.333\ldots = 219x=23.333…−2.333…=21
  • x=219=73x = \frac{21}9 = \frac 73x=921​=37​. Check: 7:3=2.333…7 : 3 = 2.333\ldots7:3=2.333… ✓

(c) x=0.1212…x = 0.1212\ldotsx=0.1212… has a repeating block of two digits, so I multiply by 100100100:

  • 100x=12.1212…100x = 12.1212\ldots100x=12.1212…
  • 99x=1299x = 1299x=12
  • x=1299=433x = \frac{12}{99} = \frac 4{33}x=9912​=334​.

3 · 0.9‾=10.\overline 9 = 10.9=1 with the method of exercise 2 basic

Use the same method to show that 0.999…=10.999\ldots = 10.999…=1, and then that 5.9739‾=5.9745.973\overline 9 = 5.9745.9739=5.974.

Solution

x=0.999…x = 0.999\ldotsx=0.999…, so 10x=9.999…10x = 9.999\ldots10x=9.999… and 9x=99x = 99x=9: x=1x = 1x=1.

For the second: 5.9739‾=5.973+0.0009‾5.973\overline 9 = 5.973 + 0.000\overline 95.9739=5.973+0.0009, and 0.0009‾=0.9‾1000=11000=0.0010.000\overline 9 = \frac{0.\overline 9}{1000} = \frac 1{1000} = 0.0010.0009=10000.9​=10001​=0.001. So 5.9739‾=5.973+0.001=5.9745.973\overline 9 = 5.973 + 0.001 = 5.9745.9739=5.973+0.001=5.974.

4 · 3\sqrt 33​ is not rational intermediate

Prove by contradiction that 3∉Q\sqrt 3 \notin \Q3​∈/Q. Hint: you need the fact "if a2a^2a2 is divisible by 3, so is aaa". Prove this too.

Solution

The fact about multiples of 3. Every integer aaa can be written in one of three ways: a=3ka = 3ka=3k, a=3k+1a = 3k + 1a=3k+1 or a=3k+2a = 3k + 2a=3k+2. In the last two cases:

  • (3k+1)2=9k2+6k+1=3(3k2+2k)+1(3k + 1)^2 = 9k^2 + 6k + 1 = 3(3k^2 + 2k) + 1(3k+1)2=9k2+6k+1=3(3k2+2k)+1: remainder 1 when divided by 3;
  • (3k+2)2=9k2+12k+4=3(3k2+4k+1)+1(3k + 2)^2 = 9k^2 + 12k + 4 = 3(3k^2 + 4k + 1) + 1(3k+2)2=9k2+12k+4=3(3k2+4k+1)+1: remainder 1.

So if aaa is not a multiple of 3, neither is a2a^2a2. Put the other way round: if a2a^2a2 is a multiple of 3, so is aaa.

The proof, as for 2\sqrt 22​:

  1. For a contradiction, 3=ab\sqrt 3 = \frac ab3​=ba​, a fraction reduced to lowest terms.
  2. Squaring: a2=3b2a^2 = 3b^2a2=3b2. So a2a^2a2 is a multiple of 3, and by the fact just seen so is aaa: a=3ka = 3ka=3k.
  3. Substituting: 9k2=3b29k^2 = 3b^29k2=3b2, that is b2=3k2b^2 = 3k^2b2=3k2. So bbb is a multiple of 3 too.
  4. aaa and bbb have the factor 3 in common: the fraction was not reduced. Contradiction, so 3∉Q\sqrt 3 \notin \Q3​∈/Q.

5 · Rational plus irrational intermediate

(a) Prove that if q∈Qq \in \Qq∈Q and x∉Qx \notin \Qx∈/Q, then q+x∉Qq + x \notin \Qq+x∈/Q. (b) Find two irrational numbers whose sum is rational, and two whose product is rational.

Solution

(a) For a contradiction, suppose q+x=rq + x = rq+x=r with r∈Qr \in \Qr∈Q. Then x=r−qx = r - qx=r−q. But the difference of two rationals is rational: ab−cd=ad−bcbd\frac ab - \frac cd = \frac{ad - bc}{bd}ba​−dc​=bdad−bc​. So x∈Qx \in \Qx∈Q, against the assumption. Contradiction: q+x∉Qq + x \notin \Qq+x∈/Q.

(b) Sum: 2+(−2)=0\sqrt 2 + (-\sqrt 2) = 02​+(−2​)=0. Product: 2⋅2=2\sqrt 2 \cdot \sqrt 2 = 22​⋅2​=2, or 2⋅8=16=4\sqrt 2 \cdot \sqrt 8 = \sqrt{16} = 42​⋅8​=16​=4. So "irrational + irrational" and "irrational · irrational" can be rational: there is no general rule.

6 · Field or not? intermediate

For each set, with the usual sum and product, say whether it is a field; if it is not, point out one failing property, with an example: (a) N\NN; (b) Z\ZZ; (c) the positive real numbers {x∈R∣x>0}\{x \in \R \mid x > 0\}{x∈R∣x>0}; (d) Q\QQ.

Solution

(a) N\NN: no. Property 4: 333 has no opposite in N\NN, because −3∉N-3 \notin \N−3∈/N.

(b) Z\ZZ: no. Property 8: 222 has no inverse in Z\ZZ, because 12∉Z\frac 12 \notin \Z21​∈/Z.

(c) Positive reals: no. Property 1: 000 is not there, so the identity element of the sum is missing (and as a consequence the opposites too).

(d) Q\QQ: yes. All nine properties hold; in particular the opposite of ab\frac abba​ is −ab\frac{-a}bb−a​ and, if a≠0a \neq 0a=0, the inverse is ba\frac baab​, which is again a fraction.

7 · Intervals basic

(a) Write with brackets the set {x∈R∣−1<x≤3}\{x \in \R \mid -1 < x \le 3\}{x∈R∣−1<x≤3}. (b) Write the interval [0,5)[0, 5)[0,5) with set notation. (c) Which interval is {x∈R∣x2<4}\{x \in \R \mid x^2 < 4\}{x∈R∣x2<4}? (d) How many elements do {0,5}\{0, 5\}{0,5} and (0,5)(0, 5)(0,5) have?

Solution

(a) (−1,3](-1, 3](−1,3]: round on the left because −1-1−1 is excluded (<<<), square on the right because 333 is included (≤\le≤).

(b) {x∈R∣0≤x<5}\{x \in \R \mid 0 \le x < 5\}{x∈R∣0≤x<5}.

(c) x2<4x^2 < 4x2<4 means that xxx lies strictly between −2-2−2 and 222: try x=1.9x = 1.9x=1.9 (3.61<43.61 < 43.61<4, yes) and x=−2x = -2x=−2 (4<44 < 44<4, no). So it is (−2,2)(-2, 2)(−2,2).

(d) {0,5}\{0, 5\}{0,5} has 2 elements; (0,5)(0, 5)(0,5) has infinitely many.

8 · Calculations without a calculator intermediate

Simplify: (a) 50\sqrt{50}50​; (b) 12⋅3\sqrt{12} \cdot \sqrt 312​⋅3​; (c) 63\frac 6{\sqrt 3}3​6​; (d) (1+2)2(1 + \sqrt 2)^2(1+2​)2; (e) 12−1\frac 1{\sqrt 2 - 1}2​−11​; (f) 33\frac{\sqrt 3}333​​ and 13\frac 1{\sqrt 3}3​1​: are they equal?

Solution

(a) 50=25⋅2=52\sqrt{50} = \sqrt{25 \cdot 2} = 5\sqrt 250​=25⋅2​=52​.

(b) 12⋅3=36=6\sqrt{12} \cdot \sqrt 3 = \sqrt{36} = 612​⋅3​=36​=6.

(c) 63=633⋅3=633=23\frac 6{\sqrt 3} = \frac{6\sqrt 3}{\sqrt 3 \cdot \sqrt 3} = \frac{6\sqrt 3}3 = 2\sqrt 33​6​=3​⋅3​63​​=363​​=23​.

(d) (1+2)2=12+2⋅1⋅2+(2)2=1+22+2=3+22(1 + \sqrt 2)^2 = 1^2 + 2 \cdot 1 \cdot \sqrt 2 + (\sqrt 2)^2 = 1 + 2\sqrt 2 + 2 = 3 + 2\sqrt 2(1+2​)2=12+2⋅1⋅2​+(2​)2=1+22​+2=3+22​.

(e) I multiply top and bottom by 2+1\sqrt 2 + 12​+1:

12−1⋅2+12+1=2+1(2)2−12=2+12−1=2+1.\frac 1{\sqrt 2 - 1} \cdot \frac{\sqrt 2 + 1}{\sqrt 2 + 1} = \frac{\sqrt 2 + 1}{(\sqrt 2)^2 - 1^2} = \frac{\sqrt 2 + 1}{2 - 1} = \sqrt 2 + 1.2​−11​⋅2​+12​+1​=(2​)2−122​+1​=2−12​+1​=2​+1.

(f) Yes: 13=33⋅3=33\frac 1{\sqrt 3} = \frac{\sqrt 3}{\sqrt 3 \cdot \sqrt 3} = \frac{\sqrt 3}33​1​=3​⋅3​3​​=33​​. In the exam quiz the same number can appear in either form.

9 · 2+3\sqrt 2 + \sqrt 32​+3​ is irrational hard

(a) Prove that 6∉Q\sqrt 6 \notin \Q6​∈/Q. (b) Use it to prove that 2+3∉Q\sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3 \notin \Q2​+3​∈/Q.

Solution

(a) For a contradiction, 6=ab\sqrt 6 = \frac ab6​=ba​ reduced. Then a2=6b2=2⋅3b2a^2 = 6b^2 = 2 \cdot 3b^2a2=6b2=2⋅3b2 is even, so aaa is even: a=2ka = 2ka=2k. Substituting: 4k2=6b24k^2 = 6b^24k2=6b2, that is 2k2=3b22k^2 = 3b^22k2=3b2. Then 3b23b^23b2 is even; since 3 is odd, b2b^2b2 must be even (odd times odd is odd), so bbb is even. aaa and bbb are both even: contradiction.

(b) For a contradiction, 2+3=q\sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3 = q2​+3​=q with q∈Qq \in \Qq∈Q. I square:

q2=(2)2+223+(3)2=5+26.q^2 = (\sqrt 2)^2 + 2\sqrt 2\sqrt 3 + (\sqrt 3)^2 = 5 + 2\sqrt 6.q2=(2​)2+22​3​+(3​)2=5+26​.

So 6=q2−52\sqrt 6 = \frac{q^2 - 5}26​=2q2−5​, which is rational because qqq is. But by part (a) 6\sqrt 66​ is not rational: contradiction. So 2+3∉Q\sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3 \notin \Q2​+3​∈/Q.

10 · The first terms of the sequence for eee basic

Compute as fractions a1a_1a1​, a2a_2a2​, a3a_3a3​, a4a_4a4​ of an=(1+1n)na_n = \left(1 + \frac 1n\right)^nan​=(1+n1​)n and check that they increase.

Solution
  • a1=21=2a_1 = 2^1 = 2a1​=21=2
  • a2=(32)2=94=2.25a_2 = \left(\frac 32\right)^2 = \frac 94 = 2.25a2​=(23​)2=49​=2.25
  • a3=(43)3=6427≈2.370a_3 = \left(\frac 43\right)^3 = \frac{64}{27} \approx 2.370a3​=(34​)3=2764​≈2.370
  • a4=(54)4=625256≈2.441a_4 = \left(\frac 54\right)^4 = \frac{625}{256} \approx 2.441a4​=(45​)4=256625​≈2.441

They increase: 2<2.25<2.370<2.4412 < 2.25 < 2.370 < 2.4412<2.25<2.370<2.441, and stay below e≈2.718e \approx 2.718e≈2.718 (see the graph in the section on the reals). Each term is rational, but the number they approach is not.

§14

Review questions

self-check

Answer out loud or in writing, then open the answer.

What do N\NN, Z\ZZ and Q\QQ contain? Is zero in N\NN?

N={0,1,2,… }\N = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}N={0,1,2,…} are the natural numbers, zero included in the course's convention. Z\ZZ adds the negatives. Q={ab∣a,b∈Z, b≠0}\Q = \{\frac ab \mid a, b \in \Z,\ b \neq 0\}Q={ba​∣a,b∈Z, b=0} contains all fractions.

Why do we go from Q\QQ to R\RR?

Because in Q\QQ there are simple equations without solutions, such as x2=2x^2 = 2x2=2, and Cauchy sequences that do not converge (for example the one defining eee). The reals fill these "holes".

What is a Cauchy sequence, in words?

An infinite list of numbers in which, from some point on, all the terms are as close to one another as you like: for every tolerance ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 there is a position NNN after which ∣am−an∣<ε|a_m - a_n| < \varepsilon∣am​−an​∣<ε.

How are the real numbers defined with Cauchy sequences?

As equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences of rationals; two sequences are equivalent if their difference tends to zero. If a sequence converges to a rational it represents that rational; otherwise it defines a new, irrational number.

What does it mean that R\RR is complete?

That every Cauchy sequence of real numbers converges to a real number: redoing the construction starting from R\RR adds nothing new.

Repeat the proof that 2\sqrt 22​ is not rational.

For a contradiction, 2=ab\sqrt 2 = \frac ab2​=ba​ reduced. Then a2=2b2a^2 = 2b^2a2=2b2, so a2a^2a2 is even and aaa is even too: a=2ka = 2ka=2k. From 4k2=2b24k^2 = 2b^24k2=2b2 we get b2=2k2b^2 = 2k^2b2=2k2, so bbb is even too. aaa and bbb are both even: the fraction was not reduced, contradiction.

What is a field? Give an example and a counterexample.

A set with two operations +++ and ⋅\cdot⋅ that have the nine properties: identities 0 and 1, opposites, inverses of the non-zero elements, commutative, associative, distributive. Examples: Q\QQ, R\RR, C\CC. Counterexample: Z\ZZ, because 2 has no inverse.

Why does zero have no inverse?

Because 0⋅x=00 \cdot x = 00⋅x=0 for every xxx: there is no xxx with 0⋅x=10 \cdot x = 10⋅x=1. This is why property 8 asks for the inverse only when a≠0a \neq 0a=0.

How is a>ba > ba>b defined?

a>ba > ba>b if a−b>0a - b > 0a−b>0. So it is enough to know which numbers are positive: in Z\ZZ they are 1,2,3,…1, 2, 3, \dots1,2,3,…; in Q\QQ the fractions with numerator and denominator of the same sign.

What is the difference between {1,2}\{1, 2\}{1,2}, (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2) and [1,2][1, 2][1,2]?

{1,2}\{1, 2\}{1,2} is the set with the two elements 1 and 2. (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2) is the open interval, endpoints excluded, or the point or vector with coordinates 1 and 2, depending on the context. [1,2][1, 2][1,2] is the closed interval, endpoints included.

Which are the nine Greek letters to know?

α\alphaα (alpha), ε\varepsilonε (epsilon), σ\sigmaσ (sigma), ϑ\varthetaϑ (theta), ϕ\phiϕ (phi), π\piπ (pi), λ\lambdaλ (lambda), μ\muμ (mu), ϱ\varrhoϱ (rho).

How do you remove a root from a denominator?

Multiply numerator and denominator by the same root: 63=633=23\frac 6{\sqrt 3} = \frac{6\sqrt 3}3 = 2\sqrt 33​6​=363​​=23​. If the denominator is a sum such as 2−1\sqrt 2 - 12​−1, multiply by 2+1\sqrt 2 + 12​+1 and use (x−y)(x+y)=x2−y2(x - y)(x + y) = x^2 - y^2(x−y)(x+y)=x2−y2.

§15

Glossary

terms
Set
A collection of objects, called elements; written with braces. Order and repetitions do not matter.
Membership (∈\in∈)
x∈Ax \in Ax∈A: xxx is an element of AAA. The opposite is written x∉Ax \notin Ax∈/A.
Subset (⊂\subset⊂, ⊊\subsetneq⊊)
B⊂AB \subset AB⊂A: every element of BBB is in AAA. B⊊AB \subsetneq AB⊊A: in addition AAA has at least one element that BBB lacks.
Natural numbers N\NN
{0,1,2,… }\{0, 1, 2, \dots\}{0,1,2,…}, zero included.
Integers Z\ZZ
{…,−2,−1,0,1,2,… }\{\dots, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, \dots\}{…,−2,−1,0,1,2,…}.
Rational numbers Q\QQ
The fractions ab\frac abba​ with a,b∈Za, b \in \Za,b∈Z and b≠0b \neq 0b=0; in decimal form they are terminating or repeating.
Real numbers R\RR
Equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences of rationals; intuitively, numbers with infinitely many digits after the decimal point.
Irrational number
A real number that is not rational, such as 2\sqrt 22​, π\piπ, eee.
Sequence
An infinite list a1,a2,a3,…a_1, a_2, a_3, \dotsa1​,a2​,a3​,…; denoted by (an)(a_n)(an​).
Cauchy sequence
A sequence whose terms, from some position on, are less than any fixed tolerance ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 apart.
Completeness
Property of R\RR: every Cauchy sequence converges. Q\QQ is not complete.
Proof by contradiction
You assume the negation of the claim is true and reach a contradiction.
Binary operation
A rule that assigns a third element to two elements, such as +++ and ⋅\cdot⋅.
Identity element
000 for the sum (a+0=aa + 0 = aa+0=a), 111 for the product (a⋅1=aa \cdot 1 = aa⋅1=a).
Opposite and inverse
The opposite of aaa is −a-a−a (a+(−a)=0a + (-a) = 0a+(−a)=0); the inverse of a≠0a \neq 0a=0 is a−1a^{-1}a−1 (a⋅a−1=1a \cdot a^{-1} = 1a⋅a−1=1).
Field
A set with +++ and ⋅\cdot⋅ having the nine properties of Proposition 1.5: Q\QQ, R\RR, C\CC yes; N\NN, Z\ZZ no.
Order
a>ba > ba>b if a−b>0a - b > 0a−b>0; R\RR is ordered, C\CC is not.
Open / closed interval
(a,b)(a, b)(a,b) excludes the endpoints, [a,b][a, b][a,b] includes them.
Quantifiers
∀\forall∀ "for all", ∃\exists∃ "there exists", ∃!\exists!∃! "there exists a unique".
